rationale: A wins because it is the more disciplined press strategy: it keeps the strongest stories tied to testable facts and names the proof before decorating the claim. Its "Figma adds a $25 seat for AI design-to-code" angle is a clean buyer-budget story, while B's otherwise useful designer angle drifts into "it lands on 4 million desks" and "fewer hours billed for it," which turns a user-count claim into labor-impact theater. A still needs a red pencil on "shippable React code," but B gives the founder more ways to get over their skis.
gaps_in_A: "Figma turns designs into shippable React code" overstates the supplied fact; the update says Make exports React and HTML/CSS as working front-end code, not that engineers can ship it.
"Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died" and "first notable product push" invent sequencing the update does not give; it only says the launch follows the collapsed acquisition.

It rejects "The future-of-work angle: how AI design assistants change creative teams" as no_journalist_shape, but a design-industry/practitioner version could be real if tied to the text-prompt layout assistant.
The Adobe-collapse angle admits it needs the collapse date, but the headline still depends on a possibly stale peg.
gaps_in_B: "it lands on 4 million desks" converts Figma's company-stated total user count into assumed exposure or adoption for the new AI assistant.
"faster work, fewer hours billed for it" invents labor and billing consequences that are not in the update.
"That silence is part of the story" makes "no IPO timing disclosed" into a capital-markets hook; that is bait unless an executive will actually engage.
"expands its addressable seat count" is an inference, not a supplied fact; it needs paying-seat or revenue context before it belongs in a deals angle.
